sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: This case study traces the evolution of my design systems practice—from early asset abstraction to fully tokenized systems—showing how foundational system thinking enabled scalability, theming, and behavioral consistency across products, platforms, and organizations.

sections.heading: Role
sections.body: Design systems lead and contributor across multiple organizations. Defined system abstractions, contracts, and governance. Partnered closely with engineering to align design intent with implementation. Mentored designers and guided system adoption and evolution.

sections.heading: System / Work
sections.body:
The work began at Roku, where supporting dozens of OEM partners required the system to handle frequent icon swaps and theming changes driven by manufacturer deals. XML-based abstraction was introduced to separate assets from implementation, enabling replacement without rewriting the system, though tooling limitations made theming and library management difficult to maintain.

At Google, the emergence of Sketch enabled a tighter bridge between design and engineering. Vector-based assets defined in JSON allowed shared SVG libraries and live specs, reducing translation loss and enabling a common source of truth.

At Amazon, the work matured into a robust tokenized design system, particularly for automotive platforms. Tokens were structured around base and semantic layers, allowing typography, color, layout, and theming to adapt through rules rather than manual updates. This approach enabled system-level capabilities such as restriction management based on rules and conditions.

This work continues through mentorship and leadership at 42, supporting designers and teams in applying tokenized systems thinking to new platforms and use cases.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body:
Enabled scalable theming and OEM customization without fragmenting systems. Reduced design–engineering friction through shared abstractions. Established token-driven rules supporting adaptive layouts and behavior. Laid the foundation for higher-level systems such as global UI surfaces and embedded AI.

With a shared design language in place, the next challenge became orchestration—how multiple surfaces and applications coexist without conflict.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: As Amazon moved to build its own operating system, window management became a critical layer of the stack. The challenge was enabling multiple applications and system surfaces to coexist—stacked, side-by-side, or overlaid—while remaining predictable, performant, and visually coherent.

sections.heading: Role
sections.body: Lead designer for the window management model. Defined system-level rules for layout, focus, and hierarchy. Partnered with platform and application engineering teams. Established contracts enabling coordination across processes.

sections.heading: System / Work
sections.body:
The work focused on creating a governed windowing framework at a high level of the OS—one that could coordinate applications that did not have direct visibility into each other.

Key aspects included directional communication between layers, z-order and priority rules, support for glassmorphic background treatments, and a responsive grid system enabling multiple applications to run concurrently across screen configurations.

Because processes were isolated, the system relied on clear contracts and signals rather than shared state, allowing complex layouts without breaking encapsulation or performance guarantees.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body:
Enabled predictable multi-window experiences at the OS level. Allowed advanced visual treatments without compromising stability. Made concurrent applications viable through clear spatial and behavioral rules. Provided a durable foundation for scalable, responsive layouts.

Once concurrency and spatial rules were established at the system level, the focus shifted to how information could surface globally without breaking application boundaries.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: The Widget Drawer is a persistent, modular UI framework that introduced global surfaces for delivering information and actions without clutter. It began with widgets on Alexa home devices and evolved to extend into mobility contexts.

sections.heading: Role
sections.body: System designer and lead for the Widget Drawer framework. Defined interaction contracts, priority rules, and governance. Partnered with engineering, product management, and business development. Enabled third-party adoption and monetization pathways.

sections.heading: System / Work
sections.body:
Widgets were treated as global surfaces rather than app-bound UI, sitting above applications to surface critical content without fragmenting flows. The framework established clear contracts, attention rules, and predictable behavior across contexts.

In partnership with product and business development, the system was opened to third-party applications, allowing sports, finance, and entertainment providers to surface timely content through widgets—creating a flywheel for engagement and monetization without compromising system integrity.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body:
Established a durable platform primitive for global UI surfaces. Enabled third-party participation through governed frameworks. Reduced cognitive load and avoided app-level interruptions. Laid the structural foundation for embedded AI.

With stable global surfaces in place, the next question became how intelligence could participate—only when appropriate—without overwhelming the system or the person.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Mobility AI focuses on embedding intelligence directly into the in-vehicle experience, allowing assistance to surface naturally without breaking flow or control.

sections.heading: Role
sections.body: Design lead for the Mobility AI interaction model. Defined how AI surfaces, escalates, and hands off information. Established rules for timing, confidence, and intervention. Partnered with engineering, product, and data teams.

sections.heading: System / Work
sections.body:
The system supports two interaction models. First, AI delivers content through dynamic cards and persistent widgets during high-confidence moments. Second, when deeper interaction is required, AI hands off to system or third-party applications to handle complex workflows.

AI intervention is governed by golden moments—brief windows where confidence is high that assistance will be useful, welcome, and safe—identified through environmental, system, behavioral, and intent signals. Criticality levels determine how prominently AI intervenes, preserving control and reversibility.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: Established a clear interaction model for embedded AI. Enabled timely assistance without distraction. Created reliable handoff patterns between AI and applications. Preserved trust through restraint and predictability.
